samples.text:
These days, many young people finish school or university but they cannot find a job easily. There are several reasons for this situation, and in this essay I will explain them and suggest what can be done to help.

The main reason is lack of experience. Most companies want to hire people who already have experience, but young graduates only have studied in the classroom. So it is like a circle: they cannot get experience without a job, and they cannot get a job without experience. Another reason is that what students learn at university is sometimes not useful for the job market. For example, many students study subjects like history or literature, but companies are looking for people with skills in technology or engineering. In addition, in some countries the economy is weak and there is not many jobs available for anyone, not only for young people.

There are some things that can help young people. Firstly, universities and colleges should work together with companies to give students internships during their study. In this way, students can get real experience and they will have more chance to get a job after graduate. Secondly, the government can give money to companies which employ young people, so that companies are more willing to hire them. Also, schools should give students better career advice, so they can choose a subject which have good job opportunities in the future.

In conclusion, young people find it difficult to get a job because they have no experience and their skills do not match what employers need. I believe that internships, government support and better advice can help them a lot to start their career.
samples.why: Reasons and help both addressed · relevant ideas but some are over-simplified · clear paragraphs with mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary · noticeable errors in tense, agreement and word form that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
In many countries, young people who have recently completed their education face considerable difficulty in finding employment. This essay will examine the main reasons for this and suggest some measures that could improve their prospects.

One major reason is the gap between the skills that young people acquire in education and those that employers actually require. Many school and university courses remains largely theoretical, so graduates may understand their subject well but lack practical abilities such as teamwork, communication or familiarity with workplace software. A related problem is the widespread demand for previous experience. Even entry-level positions often ask for one or two years of relevant work, which places young applicants in a frustrating situation where they cannot gain experience without first being employed. Finally, in periods of economic uncertainty, companies tend to reduce recruitment, and young people, who have the shortest work history, are usually the first to be affected.

To address these problems, educational institutions should work more closely with employers. Work placements and internships built into degree programmes would allow students to develop practical skills and graduate with genuine experience on their CV. Vocational courses and apprenticeships should also be given more status, since they prepare young people directly for specific careers. Governments, meanwhile, could offer financial incentives, such as reduced tax contributions, to companies that hire and train recent graduates, which would lower the risk of taking on inexperienced staff. In addition, better careers guidance in schools would help students to choose courses with realistic job prospects.

In conclusion, young people struggle to find work mainly because of a mismatch in skills, a lack of experience and weak economic conditions. Closer links between education and industry, combined with government incentives and better guidance, could make the transition from study to employment much smoother.
samples.why: Clear position · three reasons developed and linked to matching solutions · logical progression with a good range of cohesive devices · appropriate topic vocabulary (entry-level, apprenticeships) · mostly accurate with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
For many young people, the move from education into the workforce has become a prolonged and discouraging process, with months or even years passing before they secure stable employment. This difficulty has several interlocking causes, but it can be eased through closer cooperation between educators, employers and governments.

A fundamental cause is the mismatch between what education provides and what the labour market demands. Academic curricula often prioritise theoretical knowledge, leaving graduates ill-prepared for the practical and interpersonal demands of the workplace, while rapid technological change means that some skills are outdated almost as soon as they are taught. Compounding this is the so-called experience trap: employers, reluctant to invest in training, advertise even junior roles as requiring prior experience, which school leavers and graduates by definition do not possess. Structural factors play a part as well. In economies with sluggish growth, firms freeze recruitment, and because young people lack the seniority and networks of older workers, they bear a disproportionate share of the impact. The expansion of higher education has also intensified competition, as a degree no longer distinguishes an applicant in the way it once did.

Solutions should therefore target the transition itself. Embedding work placements and industry-led projects within courses would give students both relevant skills and demonstrable experience before they graduate. High-quality apprenticeships, which combine paid employment with structured training, offer an equally valuable route and deserve the same prestige as university study. Governments can reduce the risk employers perceive in hiring newcomers by subsidising wages or training costs for a limited period. Finally, careers guidance that draws on up-to-date labour market information would enable young people to make informed decisions about what to study.

In conclusion, youth unemployment stems from skills mismatches, the experience trap and wider economic weakness. By bridging the gap between education and work, societies can help young people establish themselves far more quickly.
samples.why: Reasons and solutions both fully developed and logically connected · well-managed paragraphing and cohesion · precise, flexible vocabulary (interlocking causes, experience trap, sluggish growth) · wide range of error-free structures.
